lessons.title: Life processes: what makes something alive?
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a car alive? It moves, uses fuel and gives out waste.
objectives: Recall the seven life processes
Use the life processes to decide whether something is alive
Explain why one process alone is not enough
successCriteria: Name the seven life processes (MRS GREN)
Classify things as living, dead or never alive with reasons
Argue why a car or a crystal is not alive using several processes

lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the complexity of living things; moral: respect for all life

the seven things all living organisms do

getting rid of waste made by the body

What do plants need to grow?

Process

teach.heading: Living, dead or never alive?
bullets: Never alive: never did all seven
teach.note: Sort: a wooden chair (dead: was a tree), a stone (never alive), a mushroom (living), a leaf on the ground (dead).

teach.heading: Is a car alive?
bullets: But it cannot grow, reproduce or sense
teach.note: Answer the big question as a class debate. Push for evidence: 'Which processes are missing?'

misconception.wrong: It moves, so it is alive
misconception.right: An organism must carry out all seven life processes

teach.heading: Excretion or egestion?
bullets: Excretion: waste made by cells (CO₂, urea)
Egestion: undigested food leaving the body
teach.note: Stretch point: faeces are egested, not excreted, because the food never entered our cells.

teach.heading: Check: life processes
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A crystal grows larger in a salt solution. Why is it NOT alive?
options: It only shows growth, not all seven processes
check.why: Living things must carry out all seven processes. A crystal grows but does not respire, reproduce, excrete or feed.

practice: Write the seven life processes using MRS GREN

Is a wooden spoon dead or never alive?
Give one reason a robot is not alive.
lessons.homework: Find five things at home and classify each as living, dead or never alive, giving one life process as evidence.
lessons.send: Support: MRS GREN picture cards. EAL: process words with images. Stretch: viruses debate.

lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to the air you breathe in?

keywords.def: the windpipe carrying air to the lungs
one of two tubes from the trachea into each lung

moving air into and out of the lungs

hook.text: You take about 20 000 breaths a day without thinking. What would happen if you had to remember to breathe?
hook.a: We could not sleep or concentrate; Allah made breathing automatic.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'We have certainly created the human being in the best of forms' (at-Tin 95:4). Studying the body is a way of recognising Allah's creation and of caring for the trust (amanah) of our health.

starter.q: Name the organ system that carries blood around the body.

starter.a: A group of similar cells working together.

starter.q: Which organelle releases energy in respiration?
Name the gas our cells need for respiration.

teach.heading: The airway
teach.note: Use the lung diagram picture. Rings of cartilage keep the trachea open.

teach.heading: Breathing is not respiration
bullets: Breathing: moving air in and out
Respiration: a reaction in cells releasing energy
teach.note: A very common error in exams.

misconception.right: Respiration is a chemical reaction in every cell; breathing (ventilation) moves air in and out of the lungs

teach.heading: Air in and out
bullets: Exhaled air has more carbon dioxide
teach.note: Approximate values for dry air.

teach.heading: Keeping airways clean
bullets: Cilia sweep mucus up and away
teach.note: Smoke damages cilia, so mucus builds up: smoker's cough.

teach.heading: Check

check.q: Where does air go straight after the trachea?
check.why: The trachea divides into two bronchi, one for each lung.

practice.q: Put in order: bronchioles, trachea, alveoli, bronchi.
practice.a: Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
practice.model:
Start at the widest tube: trachea.
It splits into bronchi.
Bronchi branch into bronchioles.
They end in tiny sacs: alveoli.

practice.q: How much more carbon dioxide is in exhaled air than inhaled air (use the table)?
practice.a: About 100 times more (4% against 0.04%).

practice.q: What job do cilia do?
practice.a: They sweep mucus, dust and germs up out of the airways.

independent.q: Core: Label a diagram of the gas exchange system with the five key words and one job for each (portal worksheet).
independent.a: Trachea: carries air; bronchi: into each lung; bronchioles: spread air through the lung; alveoli: gas exchange; lungs: organs of breathing.
independent.model: Teacher labels the trachea first: 'Trachea: tube held open by rings of cartilage, carries air to the bronchi.'

independent.q: Extend: Explain why breathing and respiration are different. Write in the portal response box. Start: 'Breathing is ... whereas respiration is ...'
independent.a: Breathing is moving air in and out of the lungs, whereas respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why smokers often cough in the morning.
independent.a: Smoke damages cilia, so mucus is not swept away overnight and must be coughed up.

exit.q: Gas exchange happens in the...
exit.a: Alveoli

exit.q: Big question: what happens to the air you breathe in?
exit.a: It travels down the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood.

keywords.def: a sheet of muscle under the lungs
muscles between the ribs
breathe in
breathe out
the force of gas particles pushing on a surface

hook.text: Put your hands on your ribs and breathe in deeply. What moves? What might be pulling them?
hook.a: Ribs move up and out, pulled by the intercostal muscles; the diaphragm moves down.

starter.q: Exhaled air has more... than inhaled air.
Breathing or respiration: a reaction in cells?

teach.heading: Breathing in
bullets: Intercostals pull ribs up and out
teach.note: Ask pupils to feel it as they inhale.

teach.heading: Breathing out
teach.note: Breathing out at rest is mostly relaxation.

teach.heading: Compare
teach.note: Pupils copy the table.

teach.note: Teacher demonstrates; an adult cuts the bottle at home. Pull the base down: the inside balloon inflates.

teach.heading: Check

check.q: When you breathe in, the pressure in your chest...
check.why: Volume increases, so pressure falls below the air outside and air flows in.

practice.q: Explain breathing in, in four steps.
practice.a: Diaphragm contracts and flattens; ribs move up and out; chest volume increases and pressure falls; air flows in.
practice.model: Step 1: diaphragm contracts and flattens. Step 2: intercostals pull ribs up and out. Step 3: volume up, pressure down. Step 4: air flows in from higher pressure outside.

practice.q: What does the rubber sheet represent in the model?
practice.a: The diaphragm.

practice.q: Why does air flow out when you exhale?
practice.a: Pressure inside the chest is higher than outside.

independent.q: Core: Build or watch the balloon-in-a-bottle model. Write what each part represents and what happens when you pull the base.
independent.a: Bottle: chest; balloon: lung; base sheet: diaphragm; straw: trachea. Pulling down increases volume, pressure falls, balloon inflates.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first and labels the bottle: 'The bottle is the chest (ribcage).'

independent.q: Extend: Give one strength and one weakness of the model.
independent.a: Strength: shows diaphragm changing volume. Weakness: the bottle cannot move like ribs; there is only one balloon; no alveoli.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why a hole in the chest wall can stop a lung inflating.
independent.a: Air enters the chest cavity, so pressure no longer falls when the volume increases.

exit.q: When breathing in, the diaphragm...
exit.a: Contracts and flattens

exit.q: Big question: how do your lungs fill with air when they have no muscles of their own?
exit.a: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles increase the chest volume, pressure falls and air flows in.

keywords.def: particles spreading from high to low concentration
tiny air sacs in the lungs
a tiny blood vessel with very thin walls
the total area of the outside of something
how much of a substance is in a space

hook.text: Your lungs have about the surface area of a tennis court folded inside your chest. Why might that be useful?
hook.a: A huge surface lets lots of oxygen pass into the blood quickly.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him) taught moderation: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink and a third for breath (reported by at-Tirmidhi). Islam values the breath and the health of the body.

starter.a: A sheet of muscle under the lungs.

starter.q: Name the tubes after the bronchi.

starter.a: Particles spreading from high to low concentration.

teach.heading: Swapping gases
bullets: Both move from high to low concentration
teach.note: Draw arrows on the alveolus picture.

teach.heading: Adapted for diffusion
teach.note: Each feature speeds up diffusion.

teach.heading: Damage
teach.note: This is emphysema, mainly caused by smoking.

teach.heading: Model it
teach.note: Example: oxygen levels.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Why are alveolus walls so thin?
options: So gases diffuse a short distance
check.why: A short distance makes diffusion faster.

practice.q: Which way does carbon dioxide diffuse at the alveoli, and why?
practice.a: From the blood into the alveolus, because its concentration is higher in the blood.
practice.model:
Find where it is high: carbon dioxide is high in the blood (made by respiration).
Find where it is low: the air in the alveolus.
Diffusion goes from high to low.
So blood to alveolus.

practice.q: Name two adaptations of alveoli.
practice.a: For example: large surface area; thin walls; good blood supply.

practice.q: Why do people with emphysema feel breathless?
practice.a: Damaged alveoli give less surface area, so less oxygen enters the blood.

independent.q: Core: Draw an alveolus with a capillary. Add arrows for oxygen and carbon dioxide and label three adaptations.
independent.a: Arrows: oxygen into blood, carbon dioxide out; labels: thin wall, large surface, capillary network.
independent.model: Teacher draws the first arrow: oxygen from the air sac into the capillary, labelled 'high to low'.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why a person needs millions of alveoli rather than one big sac.
independent.a: Many small sacs give a much larger surface area for the same volume, so diffusion is faster.

independent.q: Stretch: Use your breathing rate data: why does breathing rate rise during activity?
independent.a: Muscles respire faster, needing more oxygen and making more carbon dioxide, so gases must be exchanged faster.

exit.q: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the...
exit.a: Blood

exit.q: Big question: how does oxygen get from the air into your blood?
exit.a: By diffusion across the thin, moist walls of the alveoli into the capillaries.

lessons.send: SEND: alveolus diagram with arrows to complete. EAL: high, low, concentration, diffuse. Stretch: compare alveoli with villi in the small intestine.

a lower chamber that pumps blood out
a flap that stops blood flowing backwards
blood passes through the heart twice per circuit
carrying a lot of oxygen

hook.text: Your heart beats around 100 000 times a day and never rests. What makes it such a good pump?
hook.a: Thick muscular walls, four chambers and valves that keep blood flowing one way.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed in the body there is a piece of flesh which, if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart' (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The physical heart keeps the body alive; the spiritual heart keeps our faith alive.

starter.q: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the...

starter.a: Large surface area, thin walls (also good blood supply, moist).

starter.q: Which gas do cells produce in respiration?

teach.heading: Four chambers
bullets: Left side pumps to the body
Right side pumps to the lungs
teach.note: On a diagram, left and right are swapped because we look at someone else's heart.

teach.heading: The route
teach.note: Trace with a finger on the diagram.

teach.heading: Why twice?
bullets: Blood loses pressure in the lungs
Returning to the heart boosts pressure
teach.note: The left ventricle wall is thickest: it pumps furthest.

teach.heading: Valves
teach.note: Ask: what would happen with a leaky valve? Less efficient pumping.

teach.heading: Check

check.q: Which chamber pumps blood to the body?
check.why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps blood to the body.

practice.q: Describe the journey of blood from the body to the lungs.
practice.a: Body, vena cava, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs.
practice.model:
Start where blood returns: from the body into the right atrium.
Then into the right ventricle.
The right ventricle pumps it to the lungs.
So: body, right atrium, right ventricle, lungs.

practice.q: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
practice.a: It pumps blood all around the body, which needs more pressure.

practice.q: What do valves do?
practice.a: Stop blood flowing backwards.

independent.q: Core: Label the heart diagram (four chambers, valves, vessels) and colour oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.
independent.a: Left side red (oxygenated), right side blue (deoxygenated); chambers and valves labelled.
independent.model: Teacher labels the right atrium first and colours it blue: blood returning from the body has little oxygen.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why it is called a double circulation. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Blood passes through the heart twice in one full circuit: once to the lungs and once to the body.

independent.q: Stretch: Fish have a single circulation. Suggest one disadvantage.
independent.a: Blood loses pressure in the gills, so it flows slowly to the body and delivers oxygen more slowly.

exit.q: The right side of the heart pumps blood to the...
exit.a: Lungs

exit.q: Big question: why does blood go through the heart twice on each trip around the body?
exit.a: To get oxygen in the lungs and then be pumped at high pressure to the body.

practice.a: Particles gain energy, move faster and escape from the liquid as a gas.
practice.model:
What is added?
Heat energy.
What happens to particles?
They move faster.
What do they overcome?
The forces holding them in the liquid.
Result: they escape as a gas.

practice.q: Which is denser: ice or water?
practice.a: Water (ice floats).

practice.q: Name the change from gas to liquid.
practice.a: Condensing

independent.q: Core: At home put an ice cube in a glass of water and a small stone in another. Observe, then explain with particles why one floats.
independent.a: Ice floats: it is less dense than water because its particles are in an open pattern; the stone is denser and sinks.
independent.model: Teacher shows the ice in water first: it floats with most of it under the surface.

independent.q: Extend: Copy and complete: six changes of state with particle explanations.
independent.a: Melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing, subliming, deposition, each with energy gained or lost.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why floating ice helps fish survive winter.
independent.a: Ice forms on top and insulates the water below, which stays liquid.

exit.q: Most solids are... than their liquid.
exit.a: Denser

exit.q: Big question: why does ice float on water?
exit.a: Ice particles are in an open arrangement, so ice is less dense than liquid water.

lessons.send: SEND: change-of-state arrows to label. EAL: melt, boil, dense. Stretch: research dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) and sublimation.

the jerky, random movement of tiny specks in a fluid
how many particles are in a volume
with no pattern
observations that support an idea

hook.text: Someone opens a bottle of attar at the back of the masjid. Soon people at the front can smell it. How does the smell travel with no wind?
hook.a: Particles of scent move randomly and spread out: diffusion.

starter.a: Gain energy and leave fixed positions
Touch and slide past each other

teach.heading: Diffusion
teach.note: Smells spread in a room; a tea bag colours water.

teach.heading: Faster or slower?
teach.note: Particle speed explains each.

teach.heading: Brownian motion
bullets: Robert Brown, 1827: specks in water jiggled
Smoke specks in air do the same
teach.note: Einstein explained it in 1905, strong evidence for particles.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Spreading happens by chance.

misconception.wrong: Particles move to fill the space because they want to
misconception.right: Particles move randomly; by chance more move from crowded to less crowded places

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Diffusion is fastest in...
check.why: Gas particles move fast, and faster when hotter.

practice.q: Explain how a smell spreads across a room.
practice.a: Scent particles move randomly in the air and spread from high to low concentration (diffusion).
practice.model:
Name the particles: scent.
Their movement: random, fast in gas.
Direction overall: high to low concentration.
Name the process: diffusion.

practice.q: What does Brownian motion show?
practice.a: That particles in fluids are moving and bumping into visible specks.

practice.q: Why is diffusion faster when hotter?
practice.a: Particles have more energy and move faster.

independent.q: Core: Drop a tea bag into a clear glass of cold water and leave it still. Draw what you see at 0, 2 and 5 minutes and explain using particles.
independent.a: Colour spreads slowly outwards from the tea bag: diffusion from high to low concentration.
independent.model: Teacher drops the tea bag in on camera and draws the 0-minute picture: colour only around the bag.

independent.q: Extend: Predict and explain what happens with hot water (an adult pours).
independent.a: Faster spreading because particles move faster at higher temperature.

independent.q: Stretch: Why does diffusion hardly happen in solids?
independent.a: Particles are fixed in place and only vibrate, so they cannot move past each other.

exit.q: Diffusion moves particles from...
exit.a: High to low concentration

exit.q: Big question: how can you smell food cooking from another room?
exit.a: Food particles diffuse through the air by random movement from high to low concentration.

lessons.homework: Find two examples of diffusion at home and explain each in one sentence.
lessons.send: SEND: picture sequence of diffusion. EAL: spread, random, concentration. Stretch: research Einstein's 1905 explanation of Brownian motion.

hook.text: If you drop food colouring into hot and cold water at the same time, what will you see? Why?
hook.a: It spreads faster in hot water because particles move faster.

starter.a: Random jerky movement of specks in a fluid.

starter.q: Why is diffusion faster in gases?
Name a control variable in a fair test.

teach.heading: Variables
bullets: Dependent: time for colour to spread evenly
Control: volume, cup, one drop, no stirring
teach.note: Pupils fill a variables table.

teach.heading: Method
bullets: Cold tap water in cup A
Warm tap water in cup B (adult)
One drop in each at the same moment
teach.note: Model the method.

teach.heading: Safety
bullets: Food colouring stains: use a tray
teach.note: Read the safety card.

teach.heading: Example results
teach.note: Discuss.

chart.title: Time for colour to spread evenly

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: In this test the dependent variable is...
check.why: We measure the time, so it is the dependent variable.

practice.q: Write a hypothesis for this test.
practice.a: The higher the temperature, the faster the colour spreads, because particles move faster.
practice.model:
Pattern: the higher the temperature, the faster the spreading.
Reason: because the water particles have more energy and move faster, knocking the colour particles around more.
Join with 'because'.

practice.q: From the chart, how many times faster was warm than cold?
practice.a: 540 ÷ 120 = 4.5 times faster.

practice.q: Why must we not stir?
practice.a: Stirring would mix it, so we would not be measuring diffusion alone.

independent.q: Core: Carry out the test with cold and warm water. Record times and observations in the table.
independent.a: Pupils' own; warm water spreads faster.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: measure 200 ml into each cup, one drop at the same moment, start the timer.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion using your data and the particle model in the portal response box. Start: 'As temperature increased...'
independent.a: As temperature increased, the time decreased because particles moved faster and spread the colour more quickly.

independent.q: Stretch: Evaluate: name one source of error and an improvement.
independent.a: Judging 'even colour' is subjective; use a colour card or repeat and average.

exit.q: Warmer water makes diffusion...
exit.a: Faster

exit.q: Big question: does food colouring spread faster in hot or cold water?
exit.a: Hot: particles move faster, so diffusion is faster.

hook.text: Air is pushing on every square centimetre of your body right now with a force about the weight of a 1 kg bag of sugar. Why don't you feel squashed?
hook.a: The air inside your body pushes out equally.

starter.a: It is less dense than water.

teach.heading: Gas pressure
teach.note: Balloons stay inflated because particles inside hit the walls.

teach.heading: Air pressure all around

teach.note: Ears pop in aeroplanes.

bullets: Fill a glass, put card on top
Air pressure under the card holds it

check.q: What causes gas pressure?
check.why: Gas pressure is the result of many particle collisions on a surface.

practice.q: Why does a balloon get bigger when warmed?
practice.a: Particles move faster and hit the inside harder and more often, so pressure rises and stretches it.
practice.model:
Change: warmer.
Particles: move faster.
Collisions: harder and more frequent.
Pressure: rises.
Effect: the rubber stretches.

practice.q: Why do your ears pop on a plane?
practice.a: Air pressure outside changes as the plane climbs or descends.

practice.q: What is a vacuum?
practice.a: A space with no particles.

independent.q: Extend: Try the card-and-glass demo over a sink with an adult and explain it in the portal response box.
independent.a: Air pressure pushing up on the card is greater than the water pushing down.

independent.q: Stretch: Why does a sealed crisp packet puff up on a mountain?
independent.a: Air pressure outside is lower, so the higher pressure inside pushes the packet out.

exit.q: Big question: why does a card stay on an upside-down glass of water?
exit.a: Air particles push up on the card with more pressure than the water pushes down.
